items.title: CHERI under Fault Injection: An Emulation-Based Security Evaluation of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions
items.summary: Memory-safety vulnerabilities continue to dominate real-world exploit chains despite decades of research into software mitigations. CHERI is a hardware architecture that enforces spatial and temporal memory safety by augmenting pointers with hardware-checked metadata, thus preventing software-based exploitation, but its threat model explicitly excludes fault injection. This thesis investigates whether targeted fault injection can undermine CHERI's memory-safety guarantees in a pure-capability CHERI-RISC-V environment. Two fault classes are considered: bit flips corrupting capability metadata, and fault-induced check skipping on capability store instructions. We implement fault injection primitives in a QEMU-based emulation environment, which enables deterministic, repeatable experiments without specialised hardware. With them, we demonstrate four attack scenarios: buffer overflows, control-flow hijacking, data-only attacks, and use-after-free. Each succeeds with one or two targeted faults (lower bounds under the emulation-based setting). Check skipping offers an alternative route to control-flow hijacking and data-only attacks, with a minimum of one fault. These results show that CHERI's guarantees depend on the physical integrity of capability metadata, the uninterrupted execution of metadata checks, and the integrity of the revocation bitmap: a single targeted fault can circumvent spatial safety, temporal safety, or control-flow integrity. CHERI still raises the cost of exploitation, since fault injection is a prerequisite for every attack and the sentry mechanism forces an attacker to supply a valid tagged capability or spend a second fault restoring the tag. Based on these findings, we propose mitigations: ECC-protected capability memory, capability field authentication codes, redundant execution of security-critical checks, and revocation bitmap integrity verification.

items.title: Encoding, Decodability, and Use: A Five-Layer Framework for Benchmark Measurement Audits with Evidence from UAV Intent Recognition
items.summary: Benchmark accuracy is routinely read as evidence that a model understands the construct the benchmark measures. We propose and instantiate on AeroIntent a five-layer framework that decomposes that reading into observation, representation, decoding, use, and behaviour. The framework separates encoding, decodability, and use as distinct levels. In the instantiation, the observation layer is unreliable on 7 of the 20 Drone programs and floors the direct visual correlate of radial velocity at a 0.26\% scale change. The representation layer exposes two task-designed RGB features with nominal signals. RAFT flow radial bias reaches $r=+0.257$ ($p=0.030$), and bounding-box optical-flow divergence reaches $r=+0.203$ ($p=0.029$). No multi-feature readout gives a fold-mean test correlation above the cluster minimum detectable effect (MDE), and the largest positive global out-of-sample correlation is $r=+0.080$. The decoding layer sets the MDE at $|r|=0.599$ at the multi-feature Bonferroni threshold ($α=0.00714$, power 0.80), and the observed $r=+0.080$ has power 0.00. Two injection experiments establish the MDE's condition from both sides: aligned injections are detected at or above the simulated power, and orthogonal injections are not detected. The use layer finds accuracy consistent with program memory (program-identity 0.937/0.597/0.210) and multi-region static cues. The behaviour layer is consistent with accuracy not requiring a radial-velocity readout (appearance 0.6552 vs bounding-box trajectory 0.4080, cluster-level paired $Δ=+0.2471$, $p=0.0132$).

items.title: RyBench: Runtime Verification Benchmarking Framework over Publish/Subscribe Networks
items.summary: Autonomous systems built as distributed, node-based systems communicate via publish/subscribe middleware. Runtime Verification (RV) tools are used to monitor those systems against formal specifications, receiving monitored events through the pub/sub channel. An RV tool's practical value depends on its monitoring throughput capacity and verdict latency, besides its correctness, so a systematic benchmarking setup is needed to evaluate how efficiently these tools run. This paper presents RyBench, a pub/sub-based benchmarking framework that acts as a synthetic event publisher in place of a monitored system, providing a common benchmarking setup. RyBench separates benchmark generation, serialization, and transport into distinct components, enabling the combination of different event-generation strategies, data formats, and transport layers. We also evaluate the framework's throughput capacity across these configurations using Open Simulation Interface (OSI) schemas and Timescales properties, and illustrate the end-to-end benchmarking flow through an application to Reelay and an integration with MonPoly.

items.title: RehearsalBench: Can AI Predict What Happens When You Change a Company?
items.summary: Organizations increasingly ask AI systems what will happen if they change how they operate: which work to automate, which team to resize, what a voice agent will do to waiting times. We introduce RehearsalBench, a benchmark that measures whether AI models can diagnose an operation, choose an intervention, and forecast its consequences. Each model is placed in a simulated bank contact center fitted to real call-level records, sees only what a manager would see, and submits a plan and forecasts that are then played out across 200 seeded futures and three plausible versions of the organization. Decisions are scored in dollars at the stakeholders' stated valuations; forecasts are scored on the effect of each change relative to doing nothing. Ten models made 280 attempts across 14 organizations. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, improved on doing nothing by 6.8% of the no-change cost and made 77% less forecast error than a forecaster who always predicts no effect. On average, every model forecast the direction of every specified effect correctly, but models erred on the size of the same effects in the same direction, overstating a voice agent's effect on repeat contacts about five-fold. No model ever recommended holding off when doing nothing was the right choice. To test external validity, twelve models forecast 33 real organizational changes with known outcomes. Under verdict rules fixed in advance, the benchmark's forecast ranking agreed with the real-world ranking (Spearman $ρ= 0.92$, 95% lower bound 0.50). We report the result alongside an inconclusive first test, the analysis choices made after outcomes were seen, and evidence that part of the agreement reflects how well models size their uncertainty.

items.title: OmniTongue: A Comprehensive MLLM Benchmark for Automated Tongue Diagnosis in Traditional Chinese Medicine
items.summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have excelled in Western medical imaging, yet their potential in Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) tongue diagnosis remains systematically unevaluated. Tongue diagnosis requires sophisticated global and local perception, serving as a rigorous touchstone for assessing the visual understanding depth of MLLMs. However, existing datasets are limited by single dimensions, coarse granularity, and ambiguous labels, hindering the evaluation of authentic clinical capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce OmniTongue, the first comprehensive, fine-grained Visual Question Answering benchmark for TCM tongue diagnosis. This benchmark integrates 1,351 expert-validated images and 21,616 instruction pairs. Its core design features 16 clinical dimensions for multidimensional evaluation, region-specific annotations for pathological localization, and 66 fine-grained labels for precise diagnostic representation. Extensive evaluations of existing MLLMs reveal significant performance gaps, demonstrating that medical-specific models lack domain advantages, while universally poor Macro-F1 scores expose a reliance on statistical shortcuts rather than genuine understanding of tongue pathology. These findings not only highlight the current limitations of MLLMs in interpreting regional medical features but also underscore OmniTongue's significance for developing robust automated tongue diagnosis models. The code and dataset will be made publicly available in a future release.

items.title: RTLReviewBench: LLM Hardware Reviewers Rarely Miss Bugs but Routinely Reject Correct RTL
items.summary: Hardware teams increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) to review register-transfer level (RTL) code, yet it is unclear whether a model can tell a correct module from a buggy one without simulating it. We introduce RTLReviewBench, a benchmark of 114 matched pairs of buggy and correct Verilog modules. Each pair shares one specification, most buggy modules are real failures of LLM code generators, and every label is confirmed by simulation. Evaluating 12 commercial and open-weight models, we find a consistent asymmetry: reviewers rarely accept buggy code but often reject correct code, producing more than five false rejections for every missed bug. Synthetic mutants hide part of the problem: on the same designs, models miss far fewer injected bugs than real ones. Asking a model to reason before it commits to a verdict sharply reduces false rejections for weaker reviewers, and a controlled ablation shows that where the reasoning appears in the output matters more than the instruction to reason, whereas sampling and majority voting do not help. A blinded audit further shows that some correct "buggy" verdicts rest on false technical claims. We release the benchmark, a harder split for future models, all model responses, and the evaluation code at https://github.com/yasirmahmud/RTLReviewBench

items.title: AfriNORM: An Evaluation Benchmark for Normative Reasoning of LLMs Across African Cultures
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across various sectors. However, current evaluation benchmarks are insufficient to assess the applicability of these models in local African contexts, as most focus on linguistic fluency (grammar/translation) rather than cultural competence. The few existing benchmarks that measure general knowledge or social conventions do not capture the African deontic modality, i.e., the strict norms and taboos that govern diverse social interactions. In this paper, we introduce AfriNORM, a scenario-based, multiple-choice question dataset designed to measure and diagnose the normative reasoning limitations of LLMs when applied to African sociocultural contexts. We introduce two metrics: a Universal Commonsense Bias Score (UCBS) to quantify commonsense bias in LLM and a Distractor Bias Score (DBS) to quantify an LLM's limited understanding of African cultural norms. We also conduct a case study on the Yorùbá language, identifying confusion gaps in two closed-source LLMs, "Gemini 2.0 Flash" and "GPT-5", and one open-source LLM, "Llama 3.1 8B Instruct" when prompted in English versus Yorùbá. While their accuracy in English is high, their performance in Yorùbá is much lower, attributable to cultural confusion rather than simple bias, indicating that the models exhibit semantic confusion when reasoning about norms in Yorùbá.

items.title: Speeding up Automated Algorithm Design by Batch Evaluation: A Case Study of Genetic Programming for Ant Colony Optimisation
items.summary: Evaluation is becoming the bottleneck of automated algorithm design, especially for iterative algorithms such as ant colony optimisation (ACO), which must run to completion on multiple instances. A transition rule designed by genetic programming reads the construction state of each ant and must be evaluated at every step. However, existing GPU methods for ACO precompute a fixed rule and parallelise the ants of one run. To address this issue, we propose BlockEval, a batch evaluation framework with GPU and CPU backends. The GPU backend executes many runs simultaneously, each as a whole in one thread block, and compiles one module per generation. When an ant has visited all its candidate cities, a warp-cooperative fallback stalls only its warp where possible. On travelling salesman problems with 50--1000 cities, the GPU backend is 4.1--16.5 times faster than the CPU backend on 32 cores and 11.2--17.8 times faster than EvoGP+TensorACO-CL.

items.title: Exhaustive Evaluation of Fixed-Point Reciprocal Architectures for FPGAs
items.summary: Fixed-point reciprocals are used in normalization and division on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). Designs that share an output format can differ in worst-case error and in their need for memory and multipliers. The effect of table width, internal precision and refinement was evaluated for reciprocal computation in the Q16.16 and Q8.24 formats. Every representable input in the interval from 0.5 to 2.5 was tested against an exact integer reference. Five arithmetic paths were reconstructed from register-transfer-level source. Guarded interpolation, Newton-Raphson refinement and residual correction were then evaluated alongside polynomial and digit-recurrence baselines. Correct rounding was verified for all 131,073 Q16.16 and 33,554,433 Q8.24 inputs by adding one residual check to a guarded interpolated seed and one refinement step. An implementation with product reuse was verified at one input per cycle with a latency of 10 cycles in both formats. The Q8.24 implementation used nine digital signal processing slices in 7 series synthesis. The exact radix-2 control used no such slices and had a latency of 28 cycles. The reconstructed refined paths reduced the maximum relative error by factors of 205 to 223 when eight fractional bits were added. The evaluated designs provide reproducible choices for fixed accuracy budgets. In particular, correct rounding can be obtained on the tested interval by using a compact seed and checking the integer residual before the result is returned.

items.title: Information-Driven Design of Imaging Systems
items.summary: An encoder (optical system) maps objects to noiseless images, which noise corrupts into measurements. Our information estimator uses only these noisy measurements and a noise model to quantify how well measurements distinguish objects. Many imaging systems produce measurements that humans never see or cannot interpret directly. Your smartphone processes raw sensor data through algorithms before producing the final photo. MRI scanners collect frequency-space measurements that require reconstruction before doctors can view them. Self-driving cars process camera and LiDAR data directly with neural networks. What matters in these systems is not how measurements look, but how much useful information they contain. AI can extract this information even when it is encoded in ways that humans cannot interpret. And yet we rarely evaluate information content directly. Traditional metrics like resolution and signal-to-noise ratio assess individual aspects of quality separately, making it difficult to compare systems that trade off between these factors. The common alternative, training neural networks to reconstruct or classify images, conflates the quality of the imaging hardware with the quality of the algorithm. We developed a framework that enables direct evaluation and optimization of imaging systems based on their information content. In our NeurIPS 2025 paper , we show that this information metric predicts system performance across four imaging domains, and that optimizing it produces designs that match state-of-the-art end-to-end methods while requiring less memory, less compute, and no task-specific decoder design. Why mutual information? Mutual information quantifies how much a measurement reduces uncertainty about the object that produced it. Two systems with the same mutual information are equivalent in their ability to distinguish objects, even if their measurements look completely different. This single number captures the combined effect of resolution, noise, sampling, and all other factors that affect measurement quality. A blurry, noisy image that preserves the features needed to distinguish objects can contain more information than a sharp, clean image that loses those features. Information unifies traditionally separate quality metrics. It accounts for noise, resolution, and spectral sensitivity together rather than treating them as independent factors. Previous attempts to apply information theory to imaging faced two problems. The first approach treated imaging systems as unconstrained communication channels, ignoring the physical limitations of lenses and sensors. This produced wildly inaccurate estimates. The second approach required explicit models of the objects being imaged, limiting generality. Our method avoids both problems by estimating information directly from measurements. Estimating information from measurements Estimating mutual information between high-dimensional variables is notoriously difficult. Sample requirements grow exponentially with dimensionality, and estimates suffer from high bias and variance. However, imaging systems have properties that enable decomposing this hard problem into simpler subproblems. Mutual information can be written as: \[I(X; Y) = H(Y) - H(Y \mid X)\] The first term, $H(Y)$, measures total variation in measurements from both object differences and noise. The second term, $H(Y \mid X)$, measures variation from noise alone. Mutual information equals the difference between total measurement variation and noise-only variation. Imaging systems have well-characterized noise. Photon shot noise follows a Poisson distribution. Electronic readout noise is Gaussian. This known noise physics means we can compute $H(Y \mid X)$ directly, leaving only $H(Y)$ to be learned from data. For $H(Y)$, we fit a probabilistic model (e.g. a transformer or other autoregressive model) to a dataset of measurements. The model learns the distribution of all possible measurements. We tested three models spanning efficiency-accuracy tradeoffs: a stationary Gaussian process (fastest), a full Gaussian (intermediate), and an autoregressive PixelCNN (most accurate). The approach provides an upper bound on true information; any modeling error can only overestimate, never underestimate. Validation across four imaging domains Information estimates should predict decoder performance if they capture what limits real systems. We tested this relationship across four imaging applications. Information estimates predict decoder performance across color photography, radio astronomy, lensless imaging, and microscopy. Higher information consistently produces better results on downstream tasks. Color photography. Digital cameras encode color using filter arrays that restrict each pixel to detect only certain wavelengths. We compared three filter designs: the traditional Bayer pattern, a random arrangement, and a learned arrangement. Information estimates correctly ranked which designs would produce better color reconstructions, matching the rankings from neural network demosaicing without requiring any reconstruction algorithm. Radio astronomy. Telescope arrays achieve high angular resolution by combining signals from sites across the globe. Selecting optimal telescope locations is computationally intractable because each site's value depends on all others. Information estimates predicted reconstruction quality across telescope configurations, enabling site selection without expensive image reconstruction. Lensless imaging. Lensless cameras replace traditional optics with light-modulating masks. Their measurements bear no visual resemblance to scenes. Information estimates predicted reconstruction accuracy across a lens, microlens array, and diffuser design at various noise levels. Microscopy. LED array microscopes use programmable illumination to generate different contrast modes. Information estimates correlated with neural network accuracy at predicting protein expression from cell images, enabling evaluation without expensive protein labeling experiments. In all cases, higher information meant better downstream performance. Designing systems with IDEAL Information estimates can do more than evaluate existing systems. Our Information-Driven Encoder Analysis Learning (IDEAL) method uses gradient ascent on information estimates to optimize imaging system parameters. IDEAL optimizes imaging system parameters through gradient feedback on information estimates, without requiring a decoder network. The standard approach to computational imaging design, end-to-end optimization, jointly trains the imaging hardware and a neural network decoder. This requires backpropagating through the entire decoder, creating memory constraints and potential optimization difficulties. IDEAL avoids these problems by optimizing the encoder alone. We tested it on color filter design. Starting from a random filter arrangement, IDEAL progressively improved the design. The final result matched end-to-end optimization in both information content and reconstruction quality. IDEAL matches end-to-end optimization performance while avoiding decoder complexity during training. Implications Information-based evaluation creates new possibilities for rigorous assessment of imaging systems in real-world conditions. Current approaches require either subjective visual assessment, ground truth data that is unavailable in deployment, or isolated metrics that miss overall capability. Our method provides an objective, unified metric from measurements alone. The computational efficiency of IDEAL suggests possibilities for designing imaging systems that were previously intractable. By avoiding decoder backpropagation, the approach reduces memory requirements and training complexity. We explore these capabilities more extensively in follow-on work . The framework may extend beyond imaging to other sensing domains. Any system that can be modeled as deterministic encoding with known noise characteristics could benefit from information-based evaluation and design, including electronic, biological, and chemical sensors. This post is based on our NeurIPS 2025 paper "Information-driven design of imaging systems" . Code is available on GitHub . A video summary is available on the project website .

items.title: MM-ReportBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Multimodal Report Generation from Tables
items.summary: The ability to generate multimodal reports integrating fluent narratives with faithful visualizations from tabular data, has become a cornerstone capability for modern vision-language models in practical domains such as finance, healthcare, and policy making. However, existing benchmarks are limited by single-modality focus, simplistic metrics, novelty evaluation, and visualization quality. We address these limitations with MM-ReportBench, a multimodal report evaluation benchmark covering 386 tasks across 185 real-world tables. Each task is paired with an expert-curated reference report featuring standardized chapter structures and verifiable key insight points, constructed through a hybrid pipeline of multimodal reports generation based on Monte Carlo Tree Search and rigorous human quality control. For robust evaluation, we design a dual-judge evaluation framework: Text Judge Model assesses textual quality along structural completeness, grounded insight verification with numerical fact-checking against source tables, and novelty analysis that distinguishes genuine analytical discovery from trivial paraphrasing; Visualization Judge Model evaluates generated visualizations across data fidelity, expressiveness, aesthetics, and technical correctness. They also evaluate cross-modal consistency. Extensive experiments on 20 state-of-the-art models reveal critical weaknesses: even the strongest model achieves only 68.9 overall score, with numerical hallucination affecting 38.5% of reports and genuinely novel insights remaining rare. Our ablation studies further demonstrate that single-judge evaluation consistently inflates scores by 8-12 points compared to dual-judge assessment, confirming that rigorous and reliable benchmarking demands multi-faceted, complementary evaluation probes.

items.title: Cross-cultural Adaptation of Recipes for Low-Resource Languages: A Benchmark and Multilingual Culinary Lexicon for Hausa, Yorùbá, and Igbo
items.summary: Recent multilingual large language models (LLMs) have improved machine translation, yet culturally adaptive translation for low-resource languages (LRLs) remains underexplored. This is particularly challenging for recipes, where ingredients, cooking tools, measurements, and procedures may require adaptation to the target cultural context. In this work, we introduce ReciLoReL, a benchmark of 600 expert-translated and culturally adapted recipes across Yorùbá, Hausa, and Igbo (three of the most prominent languages in Nigeria), and ReciLex, a multilingual culinary lexicon containing approximately 15,000 translated entities across ten recipe entity categories, including ingredients, tools, chef actions, state of tools, and durations. We evaluate state-of-the-art multilingual LLMs for English-to-LRL recipe translation under zero-shot and few-shot settings and investigate whether augmenting LLMs with ReciLex improves culturally adaptive recipe translation without requiring large target-language recipe corpora for training or fine-tuning. Beyond conventional reference-based translation evaluation using BLEU, chrF, and TER, we introduce five criteria for evaluating cultural adaptation, adapted from established cross-cultural adaptation methods. Across the selected LLMs and languages, ReciLex improves average BLEU from 13.57 to 14.51 and chrF from 37.89 to 38.74, while reducing TER from 77.14 to 75.12. Human evaluation further shows improvements ranging from 0.11 to 0.36 points across the five cultural adaptation evaluation criteria on a five-point scale. Overall, our work provides new resources, evaluation criteria, and empirical evaluation for studying culturally adaptive recipe translation in low-resource settings.

items.title: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization
items.summary: Application optimization requires coding agents to discover useful changes and coordinate them across a complete program while preserving the required computation. We introduce Accelerate Bench, a benchmark of 32 CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions. Each task provides a working program and specifies the workload, correctness requirements, timing boundaries, and permitted edits, leaving agents to choose where and how to optimize. Public testing supports iterative development, and a separate verifier scores the final submission. On benchmark version 1.1, we evaluate 16 coding agents, each pairing a model with a harness. Their Score@1 ranges from 25.5% to 67.4%. Most of their programs are correct, and the size of the speedup separates them: the two leading agents are at least 2x faster on 22 or more of the 32 tasks, while the other fourteen reach 2x on 8 to 17 and leave 125 of their 412 correct outcomes below 1.25x. Controlled replays show why coordination across an application matters: identical source code runs between 0.29x and 2.12x depending only on build and runtime settings, and one code change is worth 1.01x or 6.4x depending on another. Accelerate Bench pairs executable workloads with agents' programs and trajectories to evaluate both their gains and the process behind them.

items.title: Dataset Distillation via Drifting
items.summary: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set of samples such that they directly approximate the per-class data distribution. Specifically, we "drift" our distilled data in the latent space of a feature extractor such that they move both toward the real data and away from each other without using a classification objective. We find that our drifted data cover the real distribution significantly better than existing methods while still serving as powerful training samples for classification. Furthermore, we showcase our method's use as a visualization tool for better interpreting models and extend it beyond images to other modalities. Our work advances the frontier of dataset distillation, offering a novel synthesis method and proposing distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation. More broadly, our findings help address the growing need to understand both data and models by uncovering more about how they interact.

items.title: Breath-Dx: A Time Series Classification Benchmark for Disease Screening with eNose
items.summary: Electronic nose (eNose) technology offers a portable, non-invasive route for disease screening via exhaled breath analysis. However, progress in the field is hindered by the lack of systematic benchmarks that compare machine learning methods under realistic conditions, particularly sensor drift, a known but rarely quantified failure mode. Most existing studies rely on small, private datasets with inconsistent protocols, rendering results non-comparable and slowing progress. We introduce Breath-Dx, the first comprehensive benchmark of time series classification methods for breath-based disease screening. Our work leverages the Scent of Health (S-OH) dataset, the largest public clinical eNose collection to date, comprising 1,234 patients across nine diagnostic groups, each providing a 17-channel multivariate time series with explicit temporal train/test splits that account for sensor drift. We systematically evaluate 10 methods spanning four families: feature-based tabular learners, convolution-based models, graph-based, and time series architectures. All methods degrade significantly under temporal validation (0.05-0.12 AUC drop compared to random cross-validation), confirming that drift embeds a strong temporal signal. Under this realistic evaluation, the best methods achieve ROC AUC of 0.74-0.76 for some lung conditions, though others remain near chance. Recurrent architectures show the most consistent performance across diseases, while specialized time series methods achieve the highest peak results. Demographic confounders matter: breath signals provide independent diagnostic value for some conditions but add little beyond age for others. We release the S-OH dataset, all temporal splits, evaluation protocols, and code to enable reproducible research and accelerate progress in clinical breathomics.

items.title: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare
items.summary: Advancing medical AI for inclusive healthcare requires evaluation across diverse healthcare roles, tasks, and care settings, but benchmark coverage remains uneven. We introduce InclusionMed, an open medical AI evaluation initiative for inclusive healthcare. The InclusionMed Atlas organizes benchmarks across three healthcare roles and three AI capabilities. For the first release, we selected four public benchmarks from 388 candidates through structured audits and independent reproduction. With InclusionMed-DxFiles, our private diagnostic reasoning benchmark, the Atlas contains five benchmarks covering three of its nine role--capability cells. We evaluated frontier large language models on the Atlas and aggregated their results into the InclusionMed Index, with overall scores ranging from 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. The Index also reports scores by healthcare role and AI capability, showing that a model's rank varied with the role or capability considered. A within-benchmark analysis using task-level tags showed that the ten highest-ranked models in the Index all scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. Models with similar Index scores also differed substantially in estimated inference cost. These findings highlight the need for evaluation covering more diverse healthcare needs and for context-specific model selection. Through open collaboration and community contributions, InclusionMed seeks to ensure that diverse healthcare needs worldwide shape how medical AI progress is defined and measured.

items.title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
items.summary: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 72% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 34%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 82-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

items.title: Contract-Explicit Evaluation: From Auditing Learned Readers to Scoped Certificates
items.summary: Evaluation readings of document-level relation extraction (DocRE) systems depend jointly on the model and the evaluation contract: gold version, scoring function, threshold. Rankings reverse across contracts, yet no existing method determines which comparisons survive the reversal. We address this gap with contract-explicit evaluation: a preregistered five-step protocol (Declare, Measure, Scope, Certify, Hedge), operationalizing the classical concordance decomposition of Kendall's rank correlation, that scopes certifiable regions and delivers distribution-free census certificates across two ecosystems. In the DocRE audit (44 training runs of one in-house architecture family), the scoring dimension scopes to a census certificate (three flagged instances, Clopper--Pearson upper bound 0.146); the confirmatory record includes registered negatives, and the audit prices its own simplification finding---the calibration dial's entire margin is one withdrawn commit. In an LLM-judge census (17 judges, 49,938 battles), 12.25% of leaderboard comparisons require hedging at the pre-declared split criterion (bound 0.124; panel-robust 0.143), with an exploratory two-tier reading certifying 69% at a bound \le 0.072 and a validity decomposition against released human labels (65% of contested battles are judge error, not ambiguity). The cross-model certificate is withdrawn on real confidence scores; the failure spectrum maps the boundary. The protocol, map, ledger, and per-instance artifacts are released.

items.title: Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in a Nigerian Cohort
items.summary: High-resolution brain MRI is important for neuroradiological assessment, yet routine clinical protocols often rely on fast, anisotropic 2D acquisitions, particularly in resource-constrained settings. These acquisitions may differ in orientation, alignment and anatomical coverage, resulting in partially overlapping image stacks. Existing learning-based super-resolution methods typically rely on single, under-constrained inputs or fixed multi-stack configurations with idealised acquisition geometry. We introduce MS-HVED, a sequence-agnostic framework for flexible multi-stack brain MRI super-resolution. Available axial, coronal and sagittal stacks are independently encoded into multi-scale Gaussian posteriors and fused using a field-of-view-aware Product-of-Gaussians formulation that limits contributions from unsupported regions. Physics-informed domain randomisation simulates heterogeneous clinical acquisition conditions, including obliqueness, partial coverage and imaging artefacts. MS-HVED achieved competitive or superior reconstruction fidelity across synthetic benchmarks and improved downstream tissue segmentation relative to low-resolution inputs. To assess generalisation beyond the training cohorts, we performed external clinical validation on 30 routine brain MRI examinations from a Nigerian cohort, representing an under-represented population in medical imaging research. These examinations formed the largest component of a blinded reader study involving 44 real cases and seven expert neuroradiologists. In the Nigerian cohort, MS-HVED was preferred over the supervised baseline for overall image quality in 187 of 210 paired assessments. Across all clinical cohorts, MS-HVED achieved higher overall-quality scores with all available inputs (5.93 vs. 4.49, p<.001), with the preference persisting when axial or coronal inputs were omitted (p<.001). items.title: SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations
items.summary: A coding agent working within a software organization must establish what to build, collaborate with colleagues, and verify what it delivers. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. Starting from a brief handoff, agents must recover requirements distributed across colleagues and workplace records, reconcile conflicting evidence, and implement changes evaluated by private executable tests. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Providing complete requirements upfront improves F2P by approximately 16 percentage points for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra, yet leaves complete task success unchanged. Requirement-level trajectory analysis reveals failures throughout the delivery process: Claude-Opus-5.5 directs a mean of 93% of first questions about queried cards to their accountable owners across runs but obtains only 64% of colleague-held requirements. Deferred questions go unfollowed, implementations remain incomplete even after requirements are acquired, and 31% of requirements reported as completed fail their tests. These findings highlight sustained requirement tracking, from clarification through implementation, verification, and handoff, as a key challenge for reliable autonomous software engineering.

items.title: GPBam: A Retrieval-Aware German Public Law Exam Benchmark
items.summary: Legal reasoning in civil-law systems is not rule-lookup: the German state examination asks for a structured opinion (Gutachten) that names the governing norms, applies them to the facts, and argues to a conclusion. We introduce GPBam (German Public Law Bar-style Exam), 81 public-law examination cases with reference solutions, paired with a recitation task over 200 statutory provisions. Drawn from state examination preparation, the cases are broad and rarely repeat, and are not publicly available - we find no evidence of exact-solution memorisation in the models we evaluate, and keeping them private limits contamination. Because each reference solution's cited norms form a retrieval gold set over the very instances the essays are graded on, GPBam scores retrieval and long-form generation jointly, which makes it a benchmark for legal retrieval as well as for legal writing and lets us ask how much retrieval quality a legal opinion actually needs. Across 32 open-weight and proprietary models evaluated without retrieval, scores span 4.81-76.42 out of 100. Supplying the law helps modestly: across seven models and eight retrieval configurations, retrieval performance varies nearly threefold and buys at most 4.1 essay points, and nothing significant for three of the seven, while an oracle with 91% gold-norm recall improves scores by 2-6 points. Essay quality strongly tracks prior knowledge: verbatim statute recall, measured in a separate task, correlates at ρ= 0.92 over 32 models.

items.title: Correct Labels Are Not Enough: Reliable Metadata Can Silently Control Model Behavior
items.summary: Fine-tuning data can include metadata that predicts the correct answer, such as a reward-model score or a quality label. We ask whether a model learns to rely on this metadata even when every training label is correct. We fine-tune 7-9B open-weight models from three families on multiple-choice questions in which (Reward: 5) always marks the correct option; when this annotation is moved to a wrong option at test time, models select that option on 97-100% of CommonsenseQA items. Removing it leaves most answers correct, so evaluation without it misses the dependence. Cue-following rises sharply with training-time reliability and develops even with neutral or nonsense annotation words, although test-time wording affects its strength. A Qwen3 experiment also finds cue dependence in option-letter scores after direct preference optimization. Audits can test for this dependence by moving or removing visible annotations while holding the task and correct answer fixed.

items.title: When Expert Disagreement Hurts: Prestige and Selectivity in LLM Decision Revision
items.summary: When language models revise a decision after another agent disagrees, neither reversal counts nor final accuracy shows whether they are fixing mistakes or abandoning correct answers. We introduce a controlled two-pass audit that holds the question, the evidence, and the model's initial answer fixed and varies only the revision context: neutral reflection, anonymous disagreement, or disagreement attributed to a domain expert. For binary decisions the accounting is exact: revision raises accuracy only if it is selective enough, reversing wrong answers more than a/(1-a) times as often as correct ones, where a is initial accuracy (nine times at 90%). Across five models and 1,989 evidence-grounded decisions in medicine, science, and law, no model clears this bar under expert disagreement, and accuracy falls by up to 16.1 points. The expert label, a prestige cue, adds reversals for four of the five models, yet its effect on accuracy ranges from a 5.2-point loss to a 2.4-point gain, so reversal counts are a poor proxy for harm. With identical arguments from both sources, the label still raises reversal for three proprietary models and in a pooled analysis of four newer models. Models also respond to stated source reliability. Revision pipelines should therefore be evaluated with paired, conditional metrics, per model and protocol.

items.summary: Wireless health monitoring system shows promise in clinical trials aconner Tue, 05/28/2019 - 13:35 Article May 30 '19 Novartis Wireless health monitoring system shows promise in clinical trials Over the past year MIT CSAIL has worked with Novartis to test a novel technology for passive, contactless monitoring of physiological signals that may be used to monitor clinical trial patients in their homes. Developed by Professor Dina Katabi and her students, the technology consists of a Wi-Fi-like device that transmits low-powered radio signals and uses machine learning algorithms to analyze their reflections and produce physiological metrics. The device can gather data on patient mobility, gait, breathing, heart rate, sleep stages, sleep apnea, and other metrics without requiring the patient to wear sensors or change their behavior in any way. Novartis and the MIT team explored the potential use of this technology in clinical trials to collect digital biomarkers, both existing and new, and potentially allow continuous, real-time monitoring of patients in their own homes. As part of the collaboration, Novartis deployed the technology in a Novartis facility, as well as in a life sciences facility with a living lab, sleep monitoring, motion and behavior monitoring. Individuals were studied for multiple days in the lab, and their motion, breathing, sleep, and behavior were measured using the technology and compared against existing standards for such measurements. Comparison to the gold standard shows that the technology has the potential to capture movement and physiological metrics, without being intrusive or requiring changes in people's behaviors . "Innovative machine learning and digital solutions, like ours, promise to change how clinical trial patients are conveniently monitored. Our collaboration with Novartis has demonstrated the potential of our touchless continuous monitoring devices, and we are thrilled about continuing to make a difference in clinical research with our cutting edge digital technology," said Katabi, Director of the MIT Center for Wireless Networks and Mobile Computing. "This collaboration with Professor Katabi's team at MIT exemplifies what like-minded academic and industry innovators can achieve in advancing exciting new digital technologies out of the laboratory and onto a path toward possible regulatory acceptance," said Jay Bradner, President of the Novartis Institutes for BioMedical Research. Katabi and Novartis are now considering next steps for further examination of this promising technology.

items.title: MIT simulator lets users design wide range of functional soft robots
items.summary: MIT simulator lets users design wide range of functional soft robots aconner Mon, 06/10/2019 - 12:37 Article June 10 '19 Adam Conner-Simons, MIT CSAIL MIT simulator lets users design wide range of functional soft robots To get robots to do things, computer scientists often use systems called physics simulators that reflect how a robot's actions will impact the real world. These simulators don't work particularly well, however, when it comes to soft robots made of flexible, deformable materials. This is because the underlying physical laws of deformable objects are much more complicated, requiring a lot more computational power to simulate. But in a new paper, a team from MIT's Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) has developed a new simulator made specifically for soft robots, and have shown that it can realistically simulate an eclectic mix of robotic designs, from a crawling robot to a four-legged running robot. The simulator doesn't just efficiently evaluate robot designs, but also provides feedback on how designs can be improved. (The system's feedback is computed based on something called "the chain rule," and so the team has dubbed the simulator "ChainQueen".) The team developed a high-performance GPU implementation of the simulator that they hope to eventually make open-source. "We believe this system has the potential to dramatically accelerate the development of soft robots," says PhD student Andrew Spielberg, one of the co-authors of the new paper being presented at the IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA). "We've also created a TensorFlow interface that will allow users at all levels to develop their own soft robotics systems without needing to understand the simulator's low-level details." ChainQueen builds off of existing techniques for simulating materials' properties going back to the "Material Point Method" (MPM) which was used to create realistic snow in the film "Frozen". Specifically, the new simulator uses a speedier form of MPM called MLS-MPM that's based on the concept of "moving least squares" (MLS), and can be more seamlessly incorporated into inference, control and co-design systems. (MLS-MPM was developed by paper co-author Yuanming Hu and researchers at the University of Pennsylvania and UCLA.) The new simulator takes MLS-MPM and makes it "differentiable," meaning that the derivative, or direction of steepest descent, can be computed for all aspects of robot control and design. This means that numerical optimizers can efficiently search for optimal robot configurations and do so much faster than recent derivative-free approaches, such as reinforcement learning. The team's project focuses specifically on elastic designs, but Hu said that future work could simulate other materials, such as plastics, cloth, or fluids, or more complex interactions with rigid and soft environments. Co-authors of the new paper include Hu, Spielberg, visiting student Jiancheng Liu, PhD student Jiajun Wu, and MIT professors Joshua B. Tenenbaum, William T. Freeman, Daniela Rus and Wojciech Matusik. items.title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
items.summary: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.

items.title: CSAIL's Daskalakis wins ACM Grace Murray Hopper Award
items.summary: CSAIL's Daskalakis wins ACM Grace Murray Hopper Award rachelg Wed, 05/08/2019 - 10:20 Article May 08 '19 Rachel Gordon Constantinos ("Costis") Daskalakis, an MIT professor and CSAIL principal investigator, has won the 2018 ACM Grace Murray Hopper Award. Constantinos ("Costis") Daskalakis, an MIT professor and CSAIL principal investigator, has won the 2018 ACM Grace Murray Hopper Award. Announced today, the prize is awarded yearly to a computer scientist on the basis of a single recent major technical or service contribution, made at or before age 35 at the time of the contribution. Daskalakis was honored for " proving that the computational complexity of finding Nash equilibria is the same as that of finding Brouwer fixed points, a proof since extended to several other equilibrium notions." "By challenging equilibrium theory, his work has triggered an ongoing reshaping of our understanding of strategic behavior, showing that computation must play an essential role in the foundations of game theory and economics." His research, a fusion of computer science, economics and game theory, focuses in part on how strategic behavior complicates large-scale technological systems. To study these systems, researchers typically use equilibrium concepts, and very prominently the concept of Nash equilibrium, which occurs when every player does the best they can given other players' choices, so no player can benefit from unilaterally changing their choice. However, Nash's equilibrium existence proof uses something called Brouwer's fixed-point theorem , for which no efficient algorithm is known. Alongside Goldberg and Papadimitriou, Daskalakis proved that the computational complexity of finding Nash equilibria is the same as that of finding Brouwer fixed points, a proof since extended to several other equilibrium notions. As such, Daskalakis's work has challenged equilibrium theory by showing that Nash equilibrium is computationally intractable and thus unattainable, in general. A native of Greece, Daskalakis received his undergraduate degree from the National Technical University of Athens and his PhD in electrical engineering and computer sciences from UC-Berkeley. He has previously received such honors as the 2018 Nevanlinna Prize from the International Mathematical Union, the 2008 ACM Doctoral Dissertation Award, the 2010 Sloan Fellowship in Computer Science, the Simons Investigator Award, and the Kalai Game Theory and Computer Science Prize from the Game Theory Society. Press mentions The National Herald Ekathimerini Costis Daskalakis 7849 Algorithms & Theory Computational Biology

metadata.readme_excerpt: # Hermes Agent ☤ Hermes Agent | Hermes Desktop **The self-improving AI agent built by [Nous Research](https://nousresearch.com).** It's the only agent with a built-in learning loop — it creates skills from experience, improves them during use, nudges itself to persist knowledge, searches its own past conversations, and builds a deepening model of who you are across sessions. Run it on a $5 VPS, a GPU cluster, or serverless infrastructure that costs nearly nothing when idle. It's not tied to your laptop — talk to it from Telegram while it works on a cloud VM. Use any model you want — [Nous Portal](https://portal.nousresearch.com), OpenRouter, OpenAI, your own endpoint, and [many others](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/integrations/providers). Switch with `hermes model` — no code changes, no lock-in. A real terminal interface Full TUI with multiline editing, slash-command autocomplete, conversation history, interrupt-and-redirect, and streaming tool output. Lives where you do Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, and CLI — all from a single gateway process. Voice memo transcription, cross-platform conversation continuity. A closed learning loop Agent-curated memory with periodic nudges. Autonomous skill creation after complex tasks. Skills self-improve during use. FTS5 session search with LLM summarization for cross-session recall. Honcho dialectic user modeling. Compatible with the agentskills.io open standard. Scheduled automations Built-in cron scheduler with delivery to any platform. Daily reports, nightly backups, weekly audits — all in natural language, running unattended. metadata.readme_excerpt: ![cover-v5-optimized](./images/GitHub_README_if.png) Dify Cloud · Self-hosting · Documentation · Dify edition overview Dify is an open-source LLM app development platform. Its intuitive interface combines AI workflow, RAG pipeline, agent capabilities, model management, observability features (including [Opik](https://www.comet.com/docs/opik/integrations/dify), [Langfuse](https://docs.langfuse.com), and [Arize Phoenix](https://docs.arize.com/phoenix)) and more, letting you quickly go from prototype to production. Here's a list of the core features: ## Quick start > Before installing Dify, make sure your machine meets the following minimum system requirements: > > - CPU >= 2 Core > - RAM >= 4 GiB The easiest way to start the Dify server is through [Docker Compose](docker/docker-compose.yaml). Install [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) with a running daemon, Docker Compose v2.35.0 or later, and OpenSSL. For a new deployment, run the following commands from the repository root. For an existing deployment, preserve your `.env` and follow the [upgrade guidance](docker/README.md#review-configuration-after-an-upgrade). ```bash cd docker cp .env.example .env openssl rand -hex 32 ``` Open `.env` and set `DIFY_AGENT_LOCAL_SANDBOX_AUTH_TOKEN` to the generated value. Keep the default `COMPOSE_PROFILES` value for the bundled services. Service defaults load automatically; no additional configuration files are required. From the same `docker` directory, start the services: ```bash docker compose up -d docker compose ps --all ``` Once the services are running, open [http://localhost/install](http://localhost/install) to complete the initial setup. metadata.readme_excerpt: Paritok A non-destructive compression gateway for coding agents — cut your input-token bill without changing your agent. Paritok sits between your agent and the LLM as a drop-in proxy. On every request it strips the tool-schema bloat, compresses tool results and file reads, and summarizes stale history — then forwards upstream, billed on the compressed tokens. Nothing is ever permanently discarded: the agent pulls back any exact original on demand. Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, OpenHands , and any agent that honors BASE_URL — you don't change a line of your agent . Powered by the first open-source 4B compression model trained specifically for coding agents (45K real agent trajectories). Cut input token bills from ~25% on turn one to past 85% in long, context-saturated sessions , and fit ~3× more turns in the same context window. metadata.readme_excerpt: # JNEEG **A brain-computer interface with a GPU on board.** Open-source 8-channel shield that turns the NVIDIA Jetson Nano into an EEG, EMG and ECG device with the TI ADS1299. [📖 Documentation](https://docs.pieeg.com/hardware/devices/jneeg/) · [🚀 How to Start](https://docs.pieeg.com/hardware/devices/jneeg/setup/) · [🛒 Buy](https://pieeg.com/jneeg/) · [💬 Discord](https://discord.gg/5Ps24p47) > [!WARNING] > JNEEG is **not a medical device** and has not been certified by any regulator for use with the human body. It is a tool for research, education and engineering. You use it at your own risk. > [!CAUTION] > **Battery only.** The Jetson Nano, the shield and everything cabled to them (monitor, keyboard) must run from a **5 V power bank** while electrodes are on a person. Never use the Jetson's wall power supply, a mains-powered monitor, or an Ethernet cable. The board has **no isolation**. Read the [Safety page](https://docs.pieeg.com/hardware/devices/jneeg/safety/) and the [liability notice](https://pieeg.com/liability/). ## At a glance | | | |---|---| | **Channels** | 8 biosignal inputs, plus reference and bias | | **Converter** | TI ADS1299, 24-bit, simultaneous sampling | | **Sample rate** | 250 SPS | | **Signals** | EEG, EMG, ECG | | **Host** | NVIDIA Jetson Nano Developer Kit | | **Link to the Jetson** | SPI on the 40-pin header, DRDY on pin 7 | | **Electrodes** | Dry or wet Ag/AgCl, 2.54 mm header | | **Power** | 5 V power bank, 3 A, up to 10,000 mAh | | **Software** | [PiEEG Server](https://github.com/pieeg-club/PiEEG-server) (`--device jneeg`), Python scripts (this repo) | ## How it works ``` Electrodes 1–8 ─┐ Reference (ear) ┼─► JNEEG ──SPI──► Jetson Nano ──► PiEEG Server Bias (ear) ─────┘ (ADS1299) (GPU) ├ dashboard :1617 ▲ ├ WebSocket :1616 5 V power bank ─────

github_projects.summary: 中文LLaMA-2 & Alpaca-2大模型二期项目 + 64K超长上下文模型 (Chinese LLaMA-2 & Alpaca-2 LLMs with 64K long context models) | **🇨🇳中文** | **🌐English** | **📖文档/Docs** | **❓提问/Issues** | **💬讨论/Discussions** | **⚔️竞技场/Arena** 本项目基于Meta发布的可商用大模型Llama-2开发,是中文LLaMA&Alpaca大模型的第二期项目,开源了**中文LLaMA-2基座模型和Alpaca-2指令精调大模型**。这些模型**在原版Llama-2的基础上扩充并优化了中文词表**,使用了大规模中文数据进行增量预训练,进一步提升了中文基础语义和指令理解能力,相比一代相关模型获得了显著性能提升。相关模型**支持FlashAttention-2训练**。标准版模型支持4K上下文长度,**长上下文版模型支持16K、64k上下文长度**。**RLHF系列模型**为标准版模型基础上进行人类偏好对齐精调,相比标准版模型在**正确价值观体现**方面获得了显著性能提升。 - 🚀 针对Llama-2模型扩充了**新版中文词表**,开源了中文LLaMA-2和Alpaca-2大模型 - 🚀 开源了预训练脚本、指令精调脚本,用户可根据需要进一步训练模型 - 🚀 使用个人电脑的CPU/GPU快速在本地进行大模型量化和部署体验 - 🚀 支持🤗transformers, llama.cpp, text-generation-webui, LangChain, privateGPT, vLLM等LLaMA生态 - 基座模型(4K上下文):Chinese-LLaMA-2 (1.3B, 7B, 13B) - 聊天模型(4K上下文):Chinese-Alpaca-2 (1.3B, 7B, 13B) - Chinese-LLaMA-2-16K (7B, 13B) 、Chinese-Alpaca-2-16K (7B, 13B) - Chinese-LLaMA-2-64K (7B)、Chinese-Alpaca-2-64K (7B) - 偏好对齐模型:Chinese-Alpaca-2-RLHF (1.3B, 7B) 中文LLaMA&Alpaca大模型 | 多模态 | Stars: 7098 | Language: Python

metadata.readme_excerpt: # [Chinese-LLaMA-Alpaca-3](https://github.com/ymcui/Chinese-LLaMA-Alpaca-3)项目启动! [**🇨🇳中文**](./README.md) | [**🌐English**](./README_EN.md) | [**📖文档/Docs**](https://github.com/ymcui/Chinese-LLaMA-Alpaca-2/wiki) | [**❓提问/Issues**](https://github.com/ymcui/Chinese-LLaMA-Alpaca-2/issues) | [**💬讨论/Discussions**](https://github.com/ymcui/Chinese-LLaMA-Alpaca-2/discussions) | [**⚔️竞技场/Arena**](http://llm-arena.ymcui.com/) 本项目基于Meta发布的可商用大模型[Llama-2](https://github.com/facebookresearch/llama)开发,是[中文LLaMA&Alpaca大模型](https://github.com/ymcui/Chinese-LLaMA-Alpaca)的第二期项目,开源了**中文LLaMA-2基座模型和Alpaca-2指令精调大模型**。这些模型**在原版Llama-2的基础上扩充并优化了中文词表**,使用了大规模中文数据进行增量预训练,进一步提升了中文基础语义和指令理解能力,相比一代相关模型获得了显著性能提升。相关模型**支持FlashAttention-2训练**。标准版模型支持4K上下文长度,**长上下文版模型支持16K、64k上下文长度**。**RLHF系列模型**为标准版模型基础上进行人类偏好对齐精调,相比标准版模型在**正确价值观体现**方面获得了显著性能提升。 #### 本项目主要内容 - 🚀 针对Llama-2模型扩充了**新版中文词表**,开源了中文LLaMA-2和Alpaca-2大模型 - 🚀 开源了预训练脚本、指令精调脚本,用户可根据需要进一步训练模型 - 🚀 使用个人电脑的CPU/GPU快速在本地进行大模型量化和部署体验 - 🚀 支持[🤗transformers](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers), [llama.cpp](https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp), [text-generation-webui](https://github.com/oobabooga/text-generation-webui), [LangChain](https://github.com/hwchase17/langchain), [privateGPT](https://github.com/imartinez/privateGPT), [vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm)等LLaMA生态 #### 已开源的模型 - 基座模型(4K上下文):Chinese-LLaMA-2 (1.3B, 7B, 13B) - 聊天模型(4K上下文):Chinese-Alpaca-2 (1.3B, 7B, 13B) - 长上下文模型(16K/64K): - Chinese-LLaMA-2-16K (7B, 13B) 、Chinese-Alpaca-2-16K (7B, 13B) - Chinese-LLaMA-2-64K (7B)、Chinese-Alpaca-2-64K (7B) - 偏好对齐模型:Chinese-Alpaca-2-RLHF (1.3B, 7B) ![](./pics/screencast.gif) ---- [中文LLaMA&Alpaca大模型](https://github.com/ymcui/Chinese-LLaMA-Alpaca) | [多模态中文LLaMA&Alpaca大模型](https://github.com/airaria/Visual-Chinese-LLaMA-Alpaca) | [多模态VLE](http

items.title: 2026 BAIR Graduate Showcase
items.summary: Congratulations to the Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research (BAIR) Lab class of 2026! This year, BAIR celebrates another remarkable group of Ph.D. graduates whose curiosity, creativity, and perseverance have pushed the frontiers of artificial intelligence and machine learning. Their work spans the breadth of modern AI — robotics and embodied intelligence, large language models and reasoning, computer vision, generative modeling, AI safety, human-AI interaction, AI for science and healthcare, and much more. Along the way, they have published influential research, built systems with real-world impact, mentored their peers, and shaped the BAIR community for the better. Now they are headed everywhere ideas travel: to faculty and postdoctoral positions, to industry research labs, and to startups of their own founding — and several are still exploring what comes next and would love to hear from you. Please join us in celebrating the achievements of these wonderful graduates. We are proud of everything they have accomplished at Berkeley, and we can't wait to see what they do next! Thank you to our friends at the Stanford AI Lab for this idea! Baifeng Shi Email: baifeng_shi@berkeley.edu Website: https://bfshi.github.io/ Advisor(s): Trevor Darrell Research Blurb: I work on building generalist vision and robotic models. What's next: Member of Technical Staff at Physical Intelligence Charlie Snell Email: csnell22@berkeley.edu Website: https://sea-snell.github.io Advisor(s): Dan Klein Research Blurb: My work aims to understand when and how the different LLM scaling paradigms can be traded off and interchanged. In particular, test-time scaling treats each prompt independently, drawing long chains of inferences and then forgetting them entirely between prompts. This differs critically from pretraining, which instead learns a compressed representation from a large dataset. I believe bridging the gap between these methods of scaling computation, presents a key open challenge in the field: how can we develop methods which turn the inferences drawn at test-time back into learned representations that the model can hold onto across interactions. Devin Guillory Email: dguillory@berkeley.edu Website: https://devinguillory.com Advisor(s): Trevor Darrell Research Blurb: Accounting for data shifts in computer vision models What's next: Building collaborative AI systems, looking for conspirators. Eve Fleisig Email: efleisig@berkeley.edu Website: https://efleisig.com Advisor(s): Dan Klein Research Blurb: I design language models to work reliably and fairly for the broad range of real LLM users. First, my research leverages disagreement among user preferences as signal, in order to train and evaluate LLMs for entire populations of users. Second, I work on designing rigorous evaluations to extricate challenging LLM harms that diverse users face. Finally, I work on core technical failures of LLMs, like miscalibrated confidence, to reduce downstream risks when models are deployed to users with different needs. Combined, these interventions facilitate building LLMs that minimize societal harms, and maximize benefits to a wider range of real-world users. What's next: Postdoctoral fellow at Princeton CITP Grace Luo Email: graceluo@berkeley.edu Website: https://graceluo.net Advisor(s): Trevor Darrell Research Blurb: My research is on interpreting and controlling generative models. For example, I've worked on re-purposing image generators for computer vision tasks, and meta-modeling language activations for better LLM probing and steering. What's next: Research scientist in industry Hanlin Zhu Email: hanlinzhu@berkeley.edu Website: https://hanlinzhu.com/ Advisor(s): Stuart Russell, Jiantao Jiao Research Blurb: My research centers on understanding and improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). What's next: Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI Haozhi Qi Email: hqi@berkeley.edu Website: https://haozhi.io/ Advisor(s): Jitendra Malik, Yi Ma Research Blurb: Dexterous Manipulation and Robot Learning What's next: Research scientist at Amazon; Faculty at University of Chicago J.D. Zamfirescu-Pereira Email: zamfi@berkeley.edu Website: https://zamfi.net Advisor(s): Bjoern Hartmann Research Blurb: My research focuses on effective human-AI co-design. I study the boundaries of language interfaces as a medium for interacting with AI, creating systems that blend language-focused interactions with structured user interfaces that draw on different levels of abstraction. I focus on language-oriented technologies, like LLMs and text-to-image models, that are powerful mediators of design processes. These technologies enable humans to describe their desires at almost any level of abstraction, from high-level goals vaguely specified ("I'd like a game to help my kid learn to read") to low-level corrections of undesired outputs ("Don't say 'I know because I've tasted it' when about a recipe substitution's taste"). What's next: Assistant Professor, Computer Science, UCLA Jiachen Lian Email: jiachenlian@berkeley.edu Website: https://jlian2.github.io Advisor(s): Gopala Anumanchipalli Research Blurb: My research focuses on human-centered AI across speech, healthcare, and systems. Looking for: Look for AI talents to join our startup Josh Kang Email: minwoo_kang@berkeley.edu Website: https://joshuaminwookang.github.io/ Advisor(s): John Canny Research Blurb: I study language modeling and related topics in NLP; specific interests are human user simulation and building conversational, collaborative AI agents. What's next: AI Scientist at Mistral AI Junhao (Bear) Xiong Email: junhao_xiong@berkeley.edu Website: https://www.linkedin.com/in/junhao-bear-xiong Advisor(s): Jennifer Listgarten, Yun Song Research Blurb: Junhao (Bear) Xiong is a PhD candidate at UC Berkeley, advised by Jennifer Listgarten and Yun S. Song. His work focuses on machine learning methods for biology, with an emphasis on generative modeling for proteins. Previously, he studied Applied Math and Computer Science at Johns Hopkins. Looking for: Research scientist Kaylo Littlejohn Email: kaylo_littlejohn@berkeley.edu Website: https://kaylolittlejohn.com Advisor(s): Gopala Anumanchipalli Research Blurb: My research is focused on speech modeling and natural language processing. I co-led the development of multimodal AI tools to accurately translate brain activity into text, audible personalized speech, and a high-fidelity "digital talking avatar" (Nature 2023, Nature Neuroscience 2025). I am also tech lead for voice modeling at Roblox. Looking for: Research Scientist / Engineer Kent Chang Email: kentkchang@berkeley.edu Website: https://kentkc.org Advisor(s): David Bamman Research Blurb: I work on NLP and multimodal machine learning, with a focus on evaluating large language models and building multimodal systems for understanding dialogue, narrative, and social interaction. My research includes benchmarks for LLM memorization, multimodal datasets sourced from feature films and television, and studies of model behavior. I'm interested in bridging computational methods with questions from the humanities and social sciences about whose voices get represented in AI systems, and about AI's broader impact. My work has appeared at EMNLP and ACL, among others. Looking for: (teaching) faculty, Research Scientist, ML/AI SWE Kevin Black Email: kvablack@berkeley.edu Website: https://kevin.black Advisor(s): Sergey Levine Research Blurb: I work on large-scale robot learning: including imitation learning, reinforcement learning, generative modeling, real-time control, and whatever else it takes to make robots work in the real world! What's next: Research Scientist of Physical Intelligence Kunhe Yang Email: kunheyang@berkeley.edu Website: https://www.kunheyang.com/ Advisor(s): Nika Haghtalab Research Blurb: My research focuses on the theoretical foundations of designing and evaluating AI algorithms in environments shaped by human incentives and AI agency. My work spans human-centric policy learning, incentive-aware evaluation, and multi-agent collaboration and information transmission, drawing on tools from machine learning theory and computational economics. What's next: Postdoc Research at Stanford Lisa Dunlap Email: lisabdunlap@berkeley.edu Website: https://lisabdunlap.com Advisor(s): Joseph Gonzalez, Trevor Darrell Research Blurb: Auditing generative models. What's next: Research Engineer at Anthropic Long (Tony) Lian Email: longlian@berkeley.edu Website: https://tonylian.com/ Advisor(s): Trevor Darrell, Adam Yala Research Blurb: My research primarily focuses on developing real-time multi-modal multi-agent systems and parallel reasoning systems through end-to-end RL. What's next: Member of Technical Staff at Thinking Machines Lab Maulik Bhatt Email: maulikbhatt@berkeley.edu Website: https://maulikb.com Advisor(s): Negar Mehr Research Blurb: My research develops autonomous robots that can safely coordinate with humans and other robots in shared environments. I build scalable algorithms grounded in game theory and diffusion models that let agents reason about the intent and behavior of others around them. My work spans real-time multi-agent trajectory planning and imitation learning in the presence of multi-modality. I've validated these methods on hardware platforms ranging from quadrotors to manipulators, with the goal of making multi-agent coordination robust, interpretable, and deployable in the real world. What's next: Joining Toyota Woven's end-to-end autonomous driving team. Michael Psenka Email: psenka@berkeley.edu Website: https://www.michaelpsenka.io/ Advisor(s): Aditi Krishnapriyan Research Blurb: Work in various domains (reinforcement learning, world models, AI+bio/chem), generally working on longer-horizon and out-of-distribution problems in planning and interpolation (e.g. robot manipulation from start state to goal, molecular dynamics of proteins between ground states). My thesis took a variational approach (think calculus of variations) directly from deep generative models of the environment, framing path-finding as minimizing a functional induced by the learned model itself (its score, its critic, or its dynamics). Through my research I've gained insight on how to properly handle dynamics in deep learning systems, and I plan to continue developing systems that are dynamic and adaptive. What's next: Lead Research Scientist at Baseten Nathan Lichtlé Email: nathan.lichtle@gmail.com Website: https://nathanlichtle.com Advisor(s): Alexandre M. Bayen Research Blurb: RL for autonomous driving. What's next: Chief Scientist & Co-founder at Yumi Health Neerja Thakkar Email: nthakkar@berkeley.edu Website: https://neerja.me/ Advisor(s): Jitendra Malik Research Blurb: My research focuses on scaling predictive world models to handle the complexity of in-the-wild motion. Using autoregressive and diffusion frameworks, I develop better representations for real-world prediction and propose methods to efficiently adapt these models to new domains. Looking for: Research scientist Nikita Mehandru Email: nmehandru@berkeley.edu Website: https://n-mehandru.github.io/ Advisor(s): Ahmed Alaa and David Bamman Research Blurb: My research develops and applies machine learning methods for clinical reasoning and disease progression modeling using unstructured text and time series data from electronic health records. In collaboration with physicians at UCSF, I bridge method development and clinical validation with the intention to build reliable, interpretable AI systems in medicine. Looking for: Research Scientist Niklas Lauffer Email: nlauffer@berkeley.edu Website: https://niklaslauffer.github.io/ Advisor(s): Stuart Russell and Sanjit Seshia Research Blurb: Niklas's research is focused on AI safety and reinforcement learning, particularly in the area of multi-agent interaction and LM agents. He's worked on enabling adversarial learning in cooperative and mixed-motive settings, solving issues of covariate shift in training LM agents on long-horizon tasks, as well as evaluating safety risks posed by LM agents in multi-agent settings. What's next: Research Scientist at Google Deepmind Qiyang Li Email: qcli@berkeley.edu Website: https://colinqiyangli.github.io/ Advisor(s): Sergey Levine Research Blurb: Recent progress in robotic manipulation policy learning has been largely driven by (1) the increasing availability of large-scale prior datasets and (2) the success of action chunking, where the policy predicts a short sequence of future actions rather than a single one. However, most action chunking policies are trained via supervised imitation learning, because efficient online self-improvement with reinforcement learning (RL) remains challenging—limiting real-world applicability. My PhD research studied how we could leverage prior data to optimize action-chunking policies with RL, combining empirical results with theoretical insights. Looking for: Post-doc/research scientist for RL in robotics and LLMs! Sampada Deglurkar Email: sampada_deglurkar@berkeley.edu Website: https://sdeglurkar.github.io/ Advisor(s): Prof Claire Tomlin Research Blurb: My research is in providing safety assurances for AI-enabled autonomous systems, ranging from robots to autonomous vehicles to aviation systems. For this, I have worked with uncertainty quantification for machine learning models, decision-making under uncertainty algorithms, and tools for producing probabilistic guarantees on system operation. Looking for: Research scientist, Research engineer Vinamra Benara Email: vbenara@berkeley.edu Website: https://cs.berkeley.edu/~vbenara Advisor(s): Ion Stoica Research Blurb: My research focuses on LLM post-training, including data curation, RLHF, RLVR with VLMs, evaluations, reasoning, agentic workflows, and interpretability. I also have strong expertise in systems infrastructure for distributed computing. Looking for: Research scientist / Research Engineer Vongani Maluleke Email: vongani_maluleke@berkeley.edu Website: https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~vongani_maluleke/ Advisor(s): Jitendra Malik and Angjoo Kanazawa Research Blurb: Vongani Maluleke is a PhD candidate at UC Berkeley (BAIR, advised by Jitendra Malik and Angjoo Kanazawa), where she led the development of MAGNet, a unified multi-agent motion generation framework that supports a wide range of motion generation tasks without retraining or architectural changes, outperforming task-specialized state-of-the-art baselines. She is currently extending this work by deploying it on a Unitree G1 humanoid to make it embody social intelligence. Before her PhD, she was a Senior AI Consultant at Deloitte, awarded Exceptional Performer two consecutive years, leading AI system development across media, telecommunications, retail, and financial services. Looking for: Research scientist Wei-Jer Chang Email: weijer_chang@berkeley.edu Website: https://weijer-chang.github.io/ Advisor(s): Masayoshi Tomizuka Research Blurb: My research focuses on developing safe and intelligent autonomous systems for complex, human-centered environments. I work at the intersection of machine learning, generative models, and reinforcement learning, with applications in autonomy. My work addresses challenges in multi-agent interaction, interactive human behavior, and long-tail safety-critical scenarios at scale. Looking for: Research Scientist, Applied Scientist, Roboticist Xiuyu Li Email: xiuyu@berkeley.edu Website: https://xiuyuli.com/ Advisor(s): Kurt Keutzer Research Blurb: My research focuses on developing scalable and self-improving large language model agents, with emphasis on coding agents for complex, long-horizon tasks. This direction builds on my work in parallel reasoning, and on broader expertise in making generative models more efficient in training and inference across language and vision. What's next: Member of Technical Staff at xAI Yichen Xie Email: yichenxie0928@gmail.com Website: https://yichen928.github.io/ Advisor(s): Masayoshi Tomizuka Research Blurb: My research focuses on building multimodal foundation models and world models that understand and interact with complex physical environments. I aim to develop unified representations across modalities, enabling AI systems to reason over space, time, and dynamics toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. What's next: Research Scientist at Luma AI Yigit Efe Erginbas Email: erginbas@berkeley.edu Website: https://www.linkedin.com/in/erginbas/ Advisor(s): Kannan Ramchandran, Thomas A.
